claims.text: Machine-learned interatomic potentials combined with efficient free-energy integration can accurately reproduce solid- and liquid-phase free energies.
The proposed method can substantially reduce computational cost relative to TOR-TILD and explicit AIMD free-energy workflows.
Established ab initio free-energy data are available for elemental and binary metals such as Al and Cu.
A limited set of high-temperature AIMD trajectories can provide adequate training configurations for both solid and liquid states.
Combining the trained potential with free-energy integration can retain vibrational entropy and anharmonic contributions.
The proposed surrogate workflow can retain electron–vibration coupling.
A temperature interval of 500–2000 K spans the melting transition for the intended test systems.
The method should initially be applicable to elemental and binary systems before extension to multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Accuracy in reproducing high-temperature atomic-force landscapes and energy surfaces governs the accuracy of phase free-energy differences.
An ML potential trained on high-fidelity ab initio data can learn the relevant high-temperature potential-energy surface.
The trained ML potential can evaluate energies and forces across relevant configurations much faster than AIMD.
The surrogate potential and free-energy integration can capture anharmonicity without the full expense of AIMD.
The surrogate potential and free-energy integration can capture electron–vibration coupling without the full expense of AIMD.
Predicted melting temperatures will agree with explicit AIMD evaluations to within a few percent.
Predicted solid–liquid free-energy differences will agree with explicit AIMD evaluations to within a few percent.
The proposed workflow will reduce computational cost by approximately 5–10 times relative to TOR-TILD.
The claimed performance requires training data that comprehensively cover the relevant high-temperature configurations.
Systems with drastic electronic-structure changes or very strong anharmonicity may require additional training data or methodological refinement.
Generalization to multicomponent high-entropy systems without substantial retraining is uncertain.
Whether the ML potential can capture all subtle entropy contributions at the desired fidelity is uncertain.
